subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm sizing the baby dragon to roughly cat scale, around 0.35m sitting height, and planning to include an egg prop beside it on the ground. Now I need to work out how to structure this using the SDK, though I don't have full visibility into its API.

I'm sorting through which builder functions are documented versus uncertain—things like joint, chain, sweep, part, membrane, and spike seem safer bets, while the exact argument shapes for paint, cards, and decal are unclear. To reduce risk I'll keep the construction fairly simple, relying on membrane for wings, spike for horns and spines, and guessing reasonable signatures for part() based on the limited examples I've seen.

Now I'm starting to think through the actual layout for a sitting dragon pose, beginning with the hips joint as the root of the hierarchy.

Mapping out joint positions...

For the broken egg, I'll build the bottom half as a lathe shape with jagged shard pieces on top, keeping it simple to avoid overcomplicating the geometry. I'm settling on flat color strings for the whole palette—teal body, amber eyes and membrane, white teeth—and for the egg speckles I'll skip surface-hit functions entirely and just place small spheres mathematically on the ellipsoid curve as a prop with no joints needed.

For the remaining details: smoke puffs become a chain of shrinking grey spheres rising from the nostril, the belly is a flattened buttery-colored sphere on the chest, the head combines a sphere and snout capsule built with aim-targeted parts, teeth are small cones along the jaw, and spines/horns use a spike helper running along the back and head.

I'm now working out joint and chain coordinates for the body in meters -- hips as root, then a spine chain of points rising upward and outward, with neck and tail built using sweeps along chain paths at set radii and colors. I'm uncertain whether chains auto-generate named joints or require explicit joints first, so I'm reasoning through how to structure the chain definitions safely.

For the limbs, I'm planning a sitting pose: legs with thighs going from hip to knee and feet planted flat on the ground, built using capsule geometry via a parent-child joint structure. I'm sketching a helper function to build capsule segments between two points with a given radius.

Setting up the color palette and module structure for the baby dragon build...

Now I'm sketching out the body in parts: torso, belly, haunches, neck chain, head, snout, and horns, all using spheres and swept cones with approximate positions and scales since the exact builder API shapes are uncertain. I'm planning teeth, jaw, eyes with pupils, and symmetric wings built from joint chains with membrane surfaces spanning leading and trailing edges between the wrist and fingertip points.

For the legs and tail I'm laying out joint chains with tapering sweep radii, finishing the tail in a flattened spade shape, and adding a row of spine spikes along the back using cones aimed outward and upward. I'm also adding nostril smoke puffs as a rising series of small spheres, and designing a broken egg prop using a lathe profile with a jagged rim plus scattered speckle spheres computed from an egg radius function, along with a helper for building the cone-shaped horns by computing length and midpoint between base and tip.

Writing speckle and smoke placement logic...

Now I'm thinking through the rigging structure—naming joints for hips, legs, and jaw while letting chains handle the neck, tail, arms, and wings automatically. I'm defining helper functions for cones, capsules, and spheres that compute midpoints and orientation so parts aim correctly between two points, then sketching out the lathe call for the egg shape, the membrane call for wing webbing, and the sweep call for tube-like body parts before writing the final assembled code.
